---
title: "xenium_nb — QC"
subtitle: "Per-cell, per-gene and per-transcript QC, one section per sample"
# Pin the kernel by name, as cluster_report.qmd does. Apptainer bind-mounts $HOME, so
# kernelspecs from ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels shadow the container's own — quarto's
# default "python3" then resolves to a host env missing the pipeline's packages, and
# every cell fails at import under `error: true` while the render still exits 0.
jupyter: python_spatial
format:
  pptx:
    reference-doc: ouhsc_ppt_template.pptx
    # `#` becomes a Section Header slide, `##` a Title-and-Content slide. Without
    # this pandoc infers the level from the headings present, so adding the first
    # `#` would silently demote every `##` to a bullet.
    slide-level: 2
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  # Keep rendering when a cell raises: one sample's panel erroring leaves an error slide
  # in its own section instead of taking the whole deck down. The cost is that a
  # genuinely broken cell yields an error slide and an exit code of 0 — read the slides,
  # not just the exit status.
  error: true
---

```{python}
# | tags: [setup]
import textwrap
import traceback
from functools import partial
from pathlib import Path

import dask
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import scanpy as sc
import spatialdata
import spatialdata_plot  # noqa: F401 — registers the .pl accessor on SpatialData
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm, Normalize


class SafeLogNorm(LogNorm):
    """LogNorm that does not re-derive its limits once both are given.

    Works around an incompatibility between spatialdata_plot and matplotlib 3.11, not
    anything about this data. spatialdata_plot calls norm.autoscale_None() with the 2D
    label array, and matplotlib's generated LogNorm.autoscale_None transforms its input
    unconditionally — even when vmin and vmax are already set — through a LogTransform
    that only accepts (N, 1). The result is
    "ValueError: Input values must have shape (N, 1) or (1,)" and no plot at all.

    Short-circuiting when both limits are known keeps the log mapping and never reaches
    the failing transform. Delete this once the two libraries agree again; a plain
    LogNorm is the intended call.
    """

    def autoscale_None(self, A):
        if self.vmin is None or self.vmax is None:
            super().autoscale_None(A)

# The reference template is 16:9 at 10 x 5.625in; leave room for a slide title.
FIGSIZE = (9.0, 4.3)
# Inches reserved beside the in-tissue plots for their colorbar, which sits outside
# the axes and would otherwise be cropped by tight_layout.
LEGEND_WIDTH = 1.4

# Deck-wide figure settings, set once here rather than per call so every slide matches.
#
# 400 dpi is chosen from the display, not from the print convention that usually
# supplies this number. These figures are 9in wide on a 10in slide, so they span 90% of
# it: a 4K screen puts 3456 pixels across that span, which needs 384 dpi. 300 (the
# offset-print number) covers 1440p and a page printed at 100%; 200 covers a 1080p
# projector and nothing above it. Matplotlib's default is 100, which is why the text
# looked soft — 7pt glyphs are about ten pixels tall before PowerPoint scales them up.
#
# The cost is roughly 4x the file size of 100 dpi, which is ~800 KB of figures for a
# two-sample deck. It grows with the cohort AND with the point count of the tissue
# scatters, so a cohort of whole-slide samples is the case where this needs revisiting.
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 400,
    "savefig.dpi": 400,
    "font.size": 8.5,
    "axes.labelsize": 8.5,
    "axes.titlesize": 8.5,
    "xtick.labelsize": 7.5,
    "ytick.labelsize": 7.5,
    "figure.titlesize": 10.5,
})

# Histogram bar fill, and the ink used for the median rule and its label. One fill for
# every panel: the four metrics are small multiples of the same measurement, not four
# series, so varying the hue would imply a distinction that does not exist.
BAR_FILL = "#7BA3CC"
ANNOTATION_INK = "#333333"
GRID_INK = "#E6E6E6"

# One colour per codeword category, fixed here so a category keeps its colour across every
# slide that draws it — the gene scatter, the rank curve and the qv distributions are read
# against each other, and a palette assigned per figure would recolour a category between
# them.
#
# Grouped by meaning rather than spread around the wheel: the two REAL gene categories are
# the deck's blue and a warm counterpart to it, and every control and unassigned class is a
# red, purple or amber. So "is this bar a gene or a control" is answered by hue family
# before any legend is read. Custom genes get the loud colour because they are the 100 in
# 5,101 that a reader is looking for.
#
# None is not a category the reader supplied — it is what the gene→category lookup returns
# for a gene with no transcript anywhere in the sample, so it cannot be mapped. Grey, and
# named as such wherever it appears.
CATEGORY_INK = {
    "predesigned_gene": BAR_FILL,
    "custom_gene": "#E08A3C",
    "deprecated_codeword": "#B07AA1",
    "negative_control_codeword": "#D1495B",
    "negative_control_probe": "#8C2F39",
    "unassigned_codeword": "#E4A11B",
    "genomic_control_probe": "#58917E",
}
UNMAPPED_INK = "#B0B0B0"

# Every raw zarr is staged into this notebook's working directory by the Nextflow
# process, so globbing is the whole input contract — no params to pass or drift.
#
# These are create_sdata's zarrs, NOT cluster_sdata's: nothing here has been filtered
# yet, which is the point. Reading this deck off clustered zarrs would show only the
# cells that survived the min_counts cut, with the discarded tail already gone — so the
# distributions would look clean no matter how much was thrown away.
ZARRS = sorted(Path(".").glob("*.zarr"))
if not ZARRS:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No .zarr directories staged next to the notebook.")

# Every per-cell QC column this deck shows, as (obs column, axis label, scale). All come
# straight from the zarr — create_sdata annotates the counts and ratios, the Xenium reader
# supplies the areas, nucleus count and segmentation method from cells.parquet. No per-cell
# or per-gene metric is derived here.
#
# This deck is exploratory: every metric appears on every plot type it can, so the whole
# panel can be looked at once and the uninformative ones dropped afterwards. That is why
# the list is long and why nothing here is packed to save space.
#
# The scale is what makes one list able to drive three different plot types. It picks the
# histogram's binning and axis, and the tissue panel's colour norm, because those are the
# same decision asked twice. The four kinds are genuinely different, not a log flag:
#
#   log          counts and areas spanning decades. Zeros cannot be drawn and are counted.
#   linear       bounded ratios and percentages. Zeros are real values and are kept — for
#                pct_control they are 87% of cells, so dropping them would empty the panel.
#   count        small integers (0–15). Binned on integer edges so each bar is one value;
#                60 logspace bins over 4 distinct values is mostly empty bars.
#   categorical  no bins and no colourbar at all — a bar chart of category counts, and a
#                discrete palette with a legend in tissue.
METRICS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts per cell", "log"),
    ("n_genes_by_transcripts", "Genes per cell", "log"),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_area", "Nucleus area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_ratio", "Nucleus / cell area", "linear"),
    ("transcripts_per_gene", "Transcripts per gene", "linear"),
    ("pct_control", "Control transcripts (%)", "linear"),
    ("control_counts", "Control transcripts per cell", "count"),
    ("nucleus_count", "Nuclei per cell", "count"),
    ("segmentation_method", "Segmentation method", "categorical"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_5_genes", "Transcripts in top 5 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_10_genes", "Transcripts in top 10 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_20_genes", "Transcripts in top 20 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_50_genes", "Transcripts in top 50 genes (%)", "linear"),
]

# Histogram panels per slide. The metrics are small multiples of one measurement rather
# than a figure each, so they stay gridded even though the tissue and scatter slides do
# not — a 2x2 is still readable at slide size, where a quarter-slide tissue panel is not.
HIST_PANELS = 4

# Which sections this deck renders. Comment a line out to drop that section; nothing else
# needs touching, and no slide function or metric list changes.
#
# The deck exists to choose the CELL and GENE filtering thresholds that cluster_sdata* will
# apply, so the two distribution sections earn their place unconditionally — they are the
# ones a cut is read off. The rest describe the run and the tissue: worth having, but not
# what a threshold is chosen from, and they are where the render time goes.
#
# Slides per sample and wall-clock cost, timed end-to-end on the two-ROI test cohort. The
# split is stark and worth knowing before enabling anything: everything that reads obs/var
# and draws with matplotlib is nearly free, while everything that rasterises the
# segmentation or pushes ~7M molecules through datashader is the entire render time.
#
#   retention           1 slide    what each candidate threshold discards      |
#   cell_distributions  1 slide    histograms of the metrics a cut is read off |
#   gene_distributions  4 slides   per-gene histograms, rank, detection        | 31 s total
#   cell_scatter       13 slides   transcripts vs genes, one per colour        | +7 s
#   transcript_stats    5 slides   qv, codeword category, per-FOV, placement   |
#   cell_tissue         4 slides   segmentation painted per metric             | these three
#   molecule_maps       4 slides   datashader over the molecule table          | ~14 min
#
# The bottom three are not separately timed; together they take the deck from ~40 s to
# ~15 min, and cell_tissue is the largest of them at 14 rasterised panels per sample.
SECTIONS = {
    "retention",
    "cell_distributions",
    "gene_distributions",
    "cell_scatter",
    "cell_tissue",
    # "transcript_stats",
    # "molecule_maps",
}

# The metrics that get a HISTOGRAM, which is a much shorter list than the ones that get a
# scatter or a tissue panel. A histogram here is a threshold tool: it exists so a cut can be
# read off it, so a metric earns one only if it IS a cut, or if it says whether a cut is the
# right instrument at all. Everything else on METRICS is still drawn — as a scatter colour
# and in tissue — it just does not also get a distribution.
#
# The cell list is the two columns cluster_sdata* actually filters on, plus the two areas.
# The areas are not thresholds anyone sets; they are here because if segmentation is broken
# then a count cut is the wrong instrument, and that has to be visible beside the counts
# rather than three slides away.
# The metrics that get a SCATTER colour, as (column, label, vmax). Four of the fourteen,
# on the same standard as the histograms: the geometry is identical on every one of these
# slides, so a colour earns a slide only if it adds a dimension the two axes do not
# already carry.
#
# Measured on a test ROI as the R^2 of predicting the colour from log(transcripts) and
# log(genes) — how much of it is just position restated:
#
#   nucleus_ratio  0.20   pct_control     0.004   <- independent, kept
#   nucleus_area   0.53   cell_area       0.60    <- mostly independent, kept
#   n_genes        0.77   pct_top_5..50   0.75-0.89  <- dropped, and the pct_top family is
#   transcripts_per_gene  0.957                      also mutually r = 0.72-0.96
#
# Dropped outright: the two columns that ARE the axes; transcripts_per_gene, which is
# exactly transcript_counts / n_genes_by_transcripts and so on log axes is distance from
# the diagonal; all four pct_transcripts_in_top_* ; nucleus_count, where 99.4% of cells
# share one value so a continuous ramp is one colour; and control_counts, which carries
# the same signal as pct_control over 14 discrete values.
#
# vmax CLIPS the colour scale, and is None where the metric is already bounded. Two of
# these have long right tails that otherwise push almost every cell to one end of the ramp
# — cell_area runs to ~1,180 against a median of 45, and pct_control is 0 for 87% of cells.
# The values are the 99th percentile rounded, so the clip discards the top ~1% of cells to
# the end colour and spends the ramp on the rest. Fixed rather than per-sample so the same
# colour means the same value across a cohort.
SCATTER_METRICS = [
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", 150),
    ("nucleus_area", "Nucleus area (µm²)", 80),
    ("nucleus_ratio", "Nucleus / cell area", None),
    ("pct_control", "Control transcripts (%)", 1.0),
]

# The metrics that get a TISSUE panel. Four of the fourteen, on the same standard again:
# a tissue panel answers "is this spatially structured or spread evenly", so a metric earns
# one only if that question changes what you would do.
#
#   transcript_counts    the column being thresholded. If low-count cells cluster at an
#                        edge or in one region they are an artefact and a global cut is the
#                        wrong tool; if they are scattered, a cut is safe.
#   cell_area            segmentation, and the companion to the above — a low-count cell
#                        that is also tiny is a fragment, not a poorly-sampled cell.
#   nucleus_ratio        the most position-independent metric in the deck (R^2 0.20 against
#                        the scatter axes), so it shows segmentation failure the counts
#                        cannot.
#   segmentation_method  categorical, and the one that reads best in tissue rather than as
#                        a distribution — on a test ROI it separates follicles from stroma
#                        by which stain segmented them.
#
# n_genes_by_transcripts is left off deliberately: it correlates with transcript_counts
# closely enough that the two panels are near-identical in space, so it costs a rasterised
# panel to restate one. The pct_top_* family, control counts and nucleus_count are off for
# the reasons given at SCATTER_METRICS.
TISSUE_METRICS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts per cell", "log"),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_ratio", "Nucleus / cell area", "linear"),
    ("segmentation_method", "Segmentation method", "categorical"),
]

CELL_HIST_METRICS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts per cell", "log"),
    ("n_genes_by_transcripts", "Genes per cell", "log"),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_area", "Nucleus area (µm²)", "log"),
]

# The per-GENE columns, same shape and same rule. A separate list because they describe a
# different population — 5,101 panel genes rather than the cells — so they cannot share a
# slide or be indexed the same way.
#
# Two, not the four create_sdata writes, because the other two are the SAME VARIABLES
# rescaled and carry no independent information (verified exactly on a test ROI, not
# approximately):
#
#   pct_dropout_by_transcripts == 100 * (1 - n_cells_by_transcripts / n_obs)
#   mean_transcripts           == total_transcripts / n_obs
#
# Plotting both members of either pair draws one distribution twice. n_cells_by_transcripts
# is kept over its rescaling because it is the column min_cells is expressed in, and
# total_transcripts over its because it is a count rather than a per-cell average.
GENE_HIST_METRICS = [
    ("n_cells_by_transcripts", "Cells detecting the gene", "log"),
    ("total_transcripts", "Transcripts per gene", "log"),
]

# The cuts cluster_sdata* applies today, drawn on the retention slide as the reference a
# candidate threshold is judged against. They are DRAWN, never applied — this deck filters
# nothing, and its whole purpose is deciding whether these two numbers are right.
#
# Keep them in step with bin/cluster_sdata.py, where they are hardcoded literals in the
# sc.pp.filter_cells / filter_genes calls rather than flags. Nothing enforces the match and
# the deck cannot import them, so a change there and not here leaves this slide quietly
# marking the wrong line.
DEFAULT_MIN_COUNTS = 10
DEFAULT_MIN_CELLS = 5

# The thresholds the retention curves label. They run well ABOVE the pipeline's current
# cut rather than bracketing it evenly, because that is where the interesting range turned
# out to be: on a test ROI min_counts=10 discards 5 cells and even 50 discards under 2%,
# so a slide that stopped near the current value would only show that nothing happens.
# Round numbers, because a threshold read off this slide should be quotable.
#
# DEFAULT_MIN_COUNTS / DEFAULT_MIN_CELLS must appear here — the current setting is drawn
# as a hollow ring among the candidates, not as its own line, so it is invisible if the
# lists do not contain it.
CANDIDATE_MIN_COUNTS = (5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500)
CANDIDATE_MIN_CELLS = (3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250)

# The molecule-table columns pulled per sample, and the quality cut drawn on the qv panel.
#
# 20 is Xenium's own default threshold — the value the decoder uses to call a transcript
# trustworthy, equivalent to a 1% error rate. This deck draws it rather than applying it,
# because Xenium already applied it: transcript_counts is built only from molecules at or
# above the cut, so the fraction below is data discarded before counting rather than a tail
# inside the counts. That fraction is the number the slide exists to report.
# The molecule-table columns materialized per sample, for the slides that aggregate in
# pandas. The MAPS do not appear here: they are drawn by spatialdata_plot straight off the
# lazy points element, so their columns never need to come into memory.
#
# feature_name is deliberately NOT here. It was only ever pulled to build the gene→category
# lookup, which create_sdata now annotates onto var — and it is the widest column in the
# table after the coordinates.
TX_COLUMNS = ["qv", "codeword_category", "fov_name",
              "overlaps_nucleus", "nucleus_distance", "z"]
QV_THRESHOLD = 20

# `size` on the datashader path is not a marker size in points — it is the handle on
# SPREADING. spatialdata_plot dilates every molecule to a disc of
# round(sqrt(size) * dpi/100) canvas points before shading, so at this deck's 400 dpi
# size=0.01 gives round(0.1 * 4) = 0 (no dilation, a molecule occupies exactly the canvas
# point it landed on) and size=1.0 gives 4 (a disc about 2.2 µm across).
#
# Dense maps take no dilation: at ~1.5 molecules per canvas point the tissue is already
# continuous, and spreading would only blur it. A very sparse map needs it to be legible
# at all — the control subset is 10,087 molecules over ~4.5M canvas points, so almost
# every occupied point holds exactly one and a single 0.56 µm point is invisible at slide
# size. Dilating does not move a molecule, it just draws it big enough to see.
#
# (This is why spreading was wrong on the fraction maps it replaced: there it inflated one
# flagged molecule into a cell-sized blob reading 100%. On a count map it is marker size.)
MAP_POINT_SIZE = 0.01
MAP_SPARSE_POINT_SIZE = 1.0

# Greyscale, deliberately, and not the viridis the cell-based tissue slides use.
#
# These maps are read for spatial STRUCTURE — where the molecules are — and fine spatial
# detail is carried almost entirely by the luminance channel; the chromatic channels have
# roughly a third of the acuity. So a ramp's usable structural contrast is its lightness
# range, and white-to-black is the widest available. Extra hues buy discrimination of
# VALUES, which is the question these slides are not asking, and a many-hue ramp with
# non-monotonic lightness would invent bands where the data is smooth.
#
# White at the bottom is load-bearing too: a count of 0 IS an empty canvas point, so the
# ramp's first colour is what "no molecules here" looks like. It has to be blank.
MAP_CMAP = "Greys"

# A constant column. The maps are drawn through the CONTINUOUS colour path — count of
# non-null values per canvas point — rather than through render_points(density=True),
# which draws the same picture but routes to the categorical shader and so never builds a
# colourbar. Colouring by a constant and reducing with "count" reaches the continuous
# shader, which does. Delete this the day density=True grows a colourbar of its own.
MAP_COUNT_COLUMN = "one_per_transcript"

# The molecule maps, as (element, label, predicate, vmax, size). Each is the SAME plot over
# a different subset of the molecule table: one call, one colormap, one reduction, differing
# only in which molecules go in and how they are scaled. The predicate runs on the lazy
# points element and its result is registered as a new element; None means the whole table.
#
# Counts rather than fractions. A fraction answers "what share of molecules here are bad",
# which is a magnitude question — and these slides are read for LOCATION. A count map at a
# low vmax is close to presence/absence, which is the encoding that question wants. It also
# sidesteps the fraction map's worst artefact, where a canvas point holding one flagged
# molecule reads as 100%.
#
# vmax differs per map because the subsets differ in density by more than an order of
# magnitude, and it is a CLIP, not a scale: everything at or above it is full black, so a
# low value turns the map into "occupied or not". The whole-table map is the exception —
# transcripts are everywhere, so its information IS the density variation that outlines
# follicles, and it needs headroom rather than clipping.
#
# These numbers are tied to this deck's FIGSIZE and 400 dpi: the datashader canvas is
# figure-inches x dpi, so counts per canvas point — and therefore vmax — change if either
# does. They were set by rendering the deck and looking, which is the only way; scaling
# them arithmetically from a different figure size does not work.
TX_MAPS = [
    ("transcripts", "All transcripts", None, 4, MAP_POINT_SIZE),
    ("below_qv", f"Below qv {QV_THRESHOLD}",
     lambda p: p["qv"] < QV_THRESHOLD, 1, MAP_POINT_SIZE),
    # Decoded, but placed in no cell. The per-cell metrics cannot see these molecules at
    # all, so a segmentation gap is invisible everywhere else in the deck.
    ("unassigned", "Assigned to no cell",
     lambda p: p["cell_id"].astype(str) == "UNASSIGNED", 2, MAP_POINT_SIZE),
    # is_gene is False for every control and unassigned codeword, so this is the whole
    # background field in one mask without naming the categories individually. Two orders
    # of magnitude sparser than the others, hence the dilation — see MAP_POINT_SIZE.
    ("control_codeword", "Control or unassigned codewords",
     lambda p: ~p["is_gene"], 1, MAP_SPARSE_POINT_SIZE),
]

# Every obs and var column this deck reads, checked against each zarr in the loop below.
# All of them come from create_sdata or the Xenium reader; none is derived here. Listing
# them in one place means a zarr that predates a column fails on the first sample with the
# column named, rather than several slides later inside whichever panel happened to want it.
#
# Deliberately the union across ALL sections, not just the enabled ones — METRICS is the
# widest list and covers SCATTER_METRICS and CELL_HIST_METRICS, which are subsets of it.
# A zarr that cannot support the whole deck should say so when it is first read, not the
# next time someone uncomments a line in SECTIONS.
REQUIRED_OBS = [col for col, _, _ in METRICS] + ["sample"]
REQUIRED_VAR = [col for col, _, _ in GENE_HIST_METRICS] + ["codeword_category"]


# ── Helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


def fit_tissue_panel(fig, ax, aspect):
    """Size a figure to one equal-aspect tissue panel and place its colourbar beside it.

    Shared by every slide that draws a spatial panel with a colourbar — the label-based
    ones and the molecule-density maps — because they have the same layout problem and
    fixing it once is the only way the two stay in step.

    Do NOT reach for tight_layout on these figures. spatialdata_plot (and fig.colorbar
    alike) attaches the colourbar as a free-standing axes that tight_layout does not know
    about, so it expands the main axes from 77% to 92% of the figure width, straight under
    the colourbar. The axes holds an equal aspect, so it cannot use that width and instead
    centres itself in the oversized box, putting the slack on its left. Positioning by hand
    is what removes the band of empty slide beside every panel.

    `aspect` is the tissue's width/height, taken from the drawn limits rather than assumed,
    so the panel fits whichever edge of the slide binds first.
    """
    # Margins in inches. The top one carries both the panel title and the suptitle, and is
    # sized for the two of them stacked — a tall sample makes a narrow figure, where the
    # suptitle wraps closer to the panel and the two would otherwise touch.
    left, top, bottom = 0.06, 0.60, 0.06
    panel_w = FIGSIZE[0] - left - LEGEND_WIDTH
    panel_h = panel_w / aspect
    # A tall sample binds on height instead, and would otherwise run off the slide.
    if panel_h + top + bottom > FIGSIZE[1]:
        panel_h = FIGSIZE[1] - top - bottom
        panel_w = panel_h * aspect
    fig_w, fig_h = left + panel_w + LEGEND_WIDTH, top + panel_h + bottom
    fig.set_size_inches(fig_w, fig_h)
    ax.set_position([left / fig_w, bottom / fig_h, panel_w / fig_w, panel_h / fig_h])
    # Re-seat the colourbar beside the panel it belongs to, since it was placed against
    # the figure the library saw rather than the one this slide ends up with. A
    # categorical metric has a legend instead and no second axes to move.
    for cax in fig.axes[1:]:
        cax.set_position([(left + panel_w + 0.12) / fig_w, bottom / fig_h,
                          0.16 / fig_w, panel_h / fig_h])


# ── Slides ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# One function per slide, each emitting its own heading, caption, and figure. The
# per-sample loop below is then literally a list of the slides in the order they appear,
# and adding or reordering one is a line there rather than a block edit. Keeping the
# caption next to the figure it describes is the other half of it — the two are edited
# together far more often than either is edited alone.


def retention_slide(sdata, sample):
    """Slide: what each candidate filtering threshold would actually discard.

    The one slide that answers the question the deck exists for. Every other panel shows
    where the distribution sits; none of them says that min_counts=10 costs 812 cells and
    25 costs 4,000. That number is close to unreadable off a log-axis histogram — it is
    the integral of the left tail, and the eye does not integrate — so it gets its own
    curve rather than being left as an exercise.

    Both panels are the survival function of the column the corresponding filter is
    expressed in: cells against `transcript_counts` for min_counts, genes against
    `n_cells_by_transcripts` for min_cells. Those are the exact columns
    sc.pp.filter_cells / filter_genes threshold, not proxies for them, so the curve is
    what the filter will do rather than an estimate of it.

    Plotted as DISCARDED rather than retained, on a log y. Retained is the intuitive
    framing but the wrong one to draw: it runs from N down to 0, so the region a threshold
    is actually chosen in — where losses are a fraction of a percent — is a flat line
    pinned to the top of the axes. Discarded on a log axis spreads exactly that region out,
    which is where the decision lives.

    A step, not a line, because the function only changes at observed values and drawing it
    smooth would imply thresholds between them behave differently. Evaluated at the unique
    observed values so it is exact — no grid, no interpolation, no binning to argue about.

    Thresholds below the smallest observed value discard nothing, and zero cannot be drawn
    on a log axis. Those are dropped rather than clamped: a curve that starts at 1 would
    claim a cut costs one object where it costs none.

    The y axis stays an absolute COUNT while the guide lines carry the percentages, rather
    than converting the axis to a share. That way the panel answers both questions without
    a second axis: the count is read off y, and "what threshold costs me 5%" is read off
    where the curve crosses a labelled guide. Percentage is the decision variable — a cut
    is chosen by what fraction it is acceptable to lose — but the count is what gets
    sanity-checked against the sample size in the title, and neither has to be computed
    from the other.
    """
    display(Markdown("## What a filtering threshold would discard"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Left, cells that a `min_counts` cut would remove; right, genes that a `min_cells` "
        "cut would remove. Both axes are log, and the curve steps at each observed value, "
        "so it is exact rather than binned. Each marked threshold is labelled with what it "
        "would cost, as a count and a share; the hollow ring is the threshold "
        "`cluster_sdata` applies today."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]
    panels = [
        (table.obs["transcript_counts"].to_numpy(dtype=float), DEFAULT_MIN_COUNTS,
         CANDIDATE_MIN_COUNTS, "min_counts",
         "Transcripts per cell (threshold)", "Cells discarded", "cells"),
        (table.var["n_cells_by_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float), DEFAULT_MIN_CELLS,
         CANDIDATE_MIN_CELLS, "min_cells",
         "Cells detecting the gene (threshold)", "Genes discarded", "genes"),
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=FIGSIZE, squeeze=False)
    for ax, (values, default, candidates, name, xlabel, ylabel, unit) in zip(
            axes.ravel(), panels):
        v = np.sort(values[np.isfinite(values)])
        # The filters keep value >= threshold, so the number discarded at t is the number
        # of values strictly below it — which is exactly searchsorted's left insertion
        # point. Evaluating at the unique observed values makes the step curve exact.
        thresholds = np.unique(v)
        discarded = np.searchsorted(v, thresholds, side="left")

        drawable = (thresholds > 0) & (discarded > 0)
        ax.step(thresholds[drawable], discarded[drawable], where="post",
                color=BAR_FILL, lw=1.6)
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        ax.set_yscale("log")

        # Candidate thresholds marked ON the curve, each labelled with what it costs. The
        # slide is read by scanning thresholds and asking what each one takes, so the
        # answer is put at the threshold rather than left to be inferred from the axes.
        # Both the count and the share are given: the share is what a cut is argued about,
        # the count is what gets sanity-checked against the sample size in the title.
        #
        # Labels sit HORIZONTALLY beside their marker, vertically centred on it, and the
        # side is chosen from where the marker falls on the axis. This exploits the one
        # thing always true of this curve: it rises monotonically, so at a marker's own
        # height the space to its right is under the curve and the space to its left is
        # above it — both empty. A horizontal label therefore never crosses the curve, and
        # staying on the marker's own line keeps it unambiguously attached to it.
        #
        # An earlier version alternated above and below with fixed offsets. It collided at
        # the low end and, worse, left several labels floating in blank space far from the
        # marker they described, so the reader had to guess the pairing.
        #
        # The flip near the right edge is what stops the high candidates running off the
        # axis: they sit far along a log x, and these labels are wide.
        x_lo, x_hi = np.log10(ax.get_xlim())

        # There is no vertical line at the pipeline's current threshold. One was drawn and
        # removed: it crossed the curve at the crowded end and made both harder to read,
        # and it duplicated a number the marker already carries. The current setting is
        # marked as a hollow ring among the candidates instead, which is why DEFAULT_* has
        # to appear in the CANDIDATE_* list for it to show at all.
        for candidate in candidates:
            lost = int(np.searchsorted(v, candidate, side="left"))
            # Nothing to mark where a threshold costs nothing; 0 cannot be drawn on a log
            # axis, and a marker at the floor would imply a cost there is none.
            if lost == 0:
                continue
            is_current = candidate == default
            ax.plot(candidate, lost, "o", ms=5.5 if is_current else 3.5,
                    markerfacecolor="white" if is_current else ANNOTATION_INK,
                    markeredgecolor=ANNOTATION_INK, markeredgewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
            to_right = (np.log10(candidate) - x_lo) / (x_hi - x_lo) < 0.55
            ax.annotate((f"{name} = " if is_current else "")
                        + f"{candidate:g} → {lost:,} ({lost / len(v):.1%})",
                        xy=(candidate, lost), xytext=(8 if to_right else -8, 0),
                        textcoords="offset points",
                        ha="left" if to_right else "right", va="center",
                        color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=6.5, zorder=3)

        ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
        ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
        ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        ax.tick_params(length=0)
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells · {table.n_vars:,} genes",
                 x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def qc_histogram_slide(sdata, sample, metrics, level="obs"):
    """Slide: this sample's QC distributions, one histogram per metric.

    `level` picks the population: "obs" for the cells, "var" for the panel genes. The two
    are the same figure over a different frame — same binning rules, same median rule,
    same zero and NaN accounting — so they share this function rather than being written
    twice and drifting.

    Hand-rolled rather than a library call, because scanpy has no histogram function.
    The other slides use sc.pl / spatialdata_plot and let those size their own marks.

    A 2x2 grid over one HIST_PANELS-sized chunk of METRICS, so adding or dropping a
    metric there changes the slides without touching this function. Leftover axes are
    removed rather than hidden — a hidden axes still reserves its cell under tight_layout
    and squeezes the real panels into a fraction of the slide.

    The binning is chosen by each metric's scale rather than shared, because the four
    kinds fail differently on each other's treatment:

      log     logspace bins, so bars are uniform width on the log axis instead of
              crowding into the left of each decade. Zeros cannot be drawn at all.
      linear  even bins over the observed range, and zeros are KEPT. They are ordinary
              values for a bounded ratio or a percentage — pct_control is 0 for 87% of
              cells, so borrowing the log panels' zero-dropping would empty the panel and
              report the emptying as a footnote.
      count   one bar per integer, on half-offset edges so each bar is centred on its
              value. nucleus_count takes four distinct values; 60 bins over it is 56
              empty bars and four spikes too thin to see.

    Cells fall off a panel two different ways, and both are counted beside the median
    rather than left to disappear — they are exactly the cells a QC deck must not hide.
    A value of zero cannot be drawn on a LOG axis (transcript_counts reaches 0 on real
    data). A value that was never measured is NaN: the reader leaves nucleus_area NaN,
    not 0, for a cell segmented without a nucleus, which is 70 of 21,724 on one ROI, and
    create_sdata's division carries that NaN into nucleus_ratio. The two are reported
    separately because they mean different things — "this cell had none" versus "this
    cell was not measured". Plotting an unmeasured cell at 0 would file it among
    genuinely cytoplasm-heavy ones.

    A categorical metric gets horizontal bars instead: there is no median to mark, no
    binning to choose, and the category names are sentences, so they belong on the axis
    that has room for them. It shares the slide with the numeric panels rather than
    taking its own, since it is the same question about the same cells.

    The styling is deliberate on three points. Bars carry a white separator, because at
    60 bins a solid fill reads as one mass and the gap is what lets neighbours be told
    apart. The left spine is dropped in favour of a recessive horizontal grid, since bar
    heights are read against gridlines and the axis line itself carries no information.
    And the median is labelled where it stands rather than in a panel title, so the
    number sits next to the rule it describes.
    """
    table = sdata.tables["table"]
    frame = table.obs if level == "obs" else table.var
    unit = "cells" if level == "obs" else "genes"

    display(Markdown(f"## Per-{unit[:-1]} QC distributions"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Distributions of "
        + ", ".join(label.lower() for _, label, _ in metrics)
        + f" across all {unit} in this sample, before any filtering. The dashed line marks "
        f"each median. Counts are on log axes, where {unit} at zero cannot be drawn; "
        "ratios and percentages are on linear axes, where zero is plotted like any other "
        f"value. {unit.capitalize()} that cannot be drawn are counted beside the median "
        "instead."
    ))

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=FIGSIZE, squeeze=False)
    for ax, (col, label, scale) in zip(axes.ravel(), metrics):
        if scale == "categorical":
            # Sorted so the axis reads as a ranking; the names are long enough that
            # alphabetical order would give the eye nothing to hold onto.
            counts = frame[col].value_counts().sort_values()
            ax.barh(range(len(counts)), counts.to_numpy(),
                    color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
            ax.set_yticks(range(len(counts)))
            # Wrapped, not truncated: these names differ in their tail (which stain), so
            # cutting them short makes the categories indistinguishable.
            ax.set_yticklabels(["\n".join(textwrap.wrap(str(c), 34)) for c in counts.index],
                               fontsize=5.5)
            ax.set_xlabel("Cells")
            ax.set_title(label, fontsize=8.5)
            ax.grid(axis="x", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
            ax.set_axisbelow(True)
            ax.tick_params(length=0)
            ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
            continue

        raw = frame[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        finite = raw[np.isfinite(raw)]

        if scale == "log":
            drawn = finite[finite > 0]
            bins = np.logspace(np.log10(drawn.min()), np.log10(drawn.max()), 60)
        elif scale == "count":
            drawn = finite
            # Half-offset integer edges, so each bar covers exactly one value.
            bins = np.arange(finite.min(), finite.max() + 2) - 0.5
        else:
            drawn = finite
            bins = np.linspace(finite.min(), finite.max(), 60)

        ax.hist(drawn, bins=bins, color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
        if scale == "log":
            ax.set_xscale("log")

        # Median over every MEASURED value, not just the plotted ones: dropping zeros is
        # a drawing constraint, and letting it move the median would misreport the sample.
        # Unmeasured cells are excluded, since they have no value to rank.
        median = float(np.median(finite))
        ax.axvline(median, color=ANNOTATION_INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")

        # Ratios and percentages need decimals; counts and areas do not, and a median of
        # "226.00" transcripts reads as a precision the metric does not have.
        note = f"median {median:,.0f}" if scale != "linear" else f"median {median:,.2f}"
        # Only counted where zeros were actually dropped, i.e. on a log axis. On a linear
        # or count panel they are drawn, so there is nothing to report.
        n_zero = len(finite) - len(drawn)
        if n_zero:
            note += f" · {n_zero:,} at zero"
        n_missing = len(raw) - len(finite)
        if n_missing:
            note += f" · {n_missing:,} not measured"
        # Anchored to the median in data coords but the top of the axes in fraction
        # coords, so the label tracks the rule horizontally and stays clear of the bars.
        ax.annotate(note, xy=(median, 1), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                    xytext=(4, -11), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=7.5)

        ax.set_xlabel(label)
        ax.set_ylabel(unit.capitalize())
        ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        ax.tick_params(length=0)
        ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

    for ax in axes.ravel()[len(metrics):]:
        fig.delaxes(ax)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(frame):,} {unit}", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def transcripts_vs_genes_slide(sdata, sample, color, label, vmax=None):
    """Slide: genes detected against transcript count, coloured by one obs column.

    The joint view the histogram slide cannot give: the two metrics are strongly coupled,
    so a cell that is unusual in the pair — many transcripts spread over few genes, or the
    reverse — sits off the main arm while looking ordinary in either margin alone.

    One slide per colour rather than a row of panels, so each scatter gets the whole
    slide. The geometry is identical every time; what changes is which cells light up.
    That is a lot of near-identical slides at METRICS' current length, and deliberately
    so — the deck is being read to decide which colours are worth keeping, which cannot
    be decided from the ones that were left out.

    Three of the colours are functions of the two axes rather than new dimensions: the
    axes themselves, and transcripts_per_gene, which on log axes is distance from the
    diagonal. They are kept because re-encoding position is not the same as showing
    nothing — the eye judges perpendicular distance poorly on log axes, and an axis
    recoloured onto itself is the reference the others are read against. The area,
    control and segmentation colours are the ones carrying genuinely independent
    information: they say whether off-arm cells are also unusual in size, in background,
    or in how they were segmented.

    A categorical colour is passed through unchanged — scanpy draws a discrete palette
    with a legend instead of a colourbar when the column is categorical, so nothing here
    branches on it. It does require the column to BE categorical, which is scanpy's own
    sanitize_anndata step on an object column, not something this deck does.

    Drawn by sc.pl.scatter with NO ax= passed. That matters: given an axes, scanpy has
    nowhere to put the colourbar and draws it on top of the data. Left to build its own
    figure it allocates a proper colourbar axes, so the size comes from
    rcParams["figure.figsize"] here instead of a figsize argument.

    Log on both axes for the same reason the histograms use it: counts span orders of
    magnitude, and on linear axes the whole cohort collapses into the bottom-left corner.
    The scale is applied afterwards because sc.pl.scatter has no log option; matplotlib
    then drops any cell at zero on either axis, so those are counted from the data and
    reported in the title rather than vanishing silently.

    `vmax` clips the colour scale, and is applied by reaching for the drawn collection
    rather than passed in: sc.pl.scatter has no vmin/vmax (verified against the installed
    scanpy), so the norm is set afterwards on the PathCollection scanpy left on the axes.
    The colourbar tracks it because it was built from that same mappable. Without the clip
    a long-tailed metric puts nearly every cell at one end of the ramp — see
    SCATTER_METRICS for which need it and why those values.
    """
    display(Markdown(f"## Transcripts vs genes — {label}"))
    display(Markdown(
        "One point per cell: transcript count against the number of genes detected in "
        f"that cell, both on log axes, coloured by {label.lower()}."
        + (f" The colour scale is clipped at {vmax:g}, so cells above that are drawn the "
           "same." if vmax is not None else "")
        + " Cells at zero on either axis cannot be drawn on a log axis and are counted in "
        "the title instead."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]
    # figsize via rc_context because scanpy builds the figure itself; see the docstring.
    with plt.rc_context({"figure.figsize": FIGSIZE}):
        sc.pl.scatter(
            table,
            x="transcript_counts",
            y="n_genes_by_transcripts",
            color=color,
            show=False,
        )

    fig = plt.gcf()
    ax = fig.axes[0]
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    # See the docstring: scanpy exposes no vmin/vmax, so the clip is set on the collection
    # it drew. vmin is left alone so the ramp still starts at the metric's own minimum.
    if vmax is not None and ax.collections:
        ax.collections[0].set_clim(vmax=vmax)
    # scanpy labels the axes with the raw obs keys; restate them in the deck's wording.
    ax.set_xlabel("Transcripts per cell")
    ax.set_ylabel("Genes detected per cell")
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)

    x = table.obs["transcript_counts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = table.obs["n_genes_by_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n_dropped = int(((x <= 0) | (y <= 0)).sum())

    title = f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells"
    if n_dropped:
        title += f" · {n_dropped:,} at zero"
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def qc_tissue_labels_slide(sdata, sample, color, label, scale):
    """Slide: the cell segmentation, coloured by one QC metric.

    Drawn with spatialdata_plot's render_labels, which paints each cell's own segmented
    footprint rather than a marker at its centroid. That is the whole reason to use it:
    a scatter needs a marker size and there is no non-arbitrary one. A constant does not
    travel between a 2,000 µm ROI and a whole slide; deriving it from cell spacing works
    but still leaves a coverage factor that is pure taste. Painting the mask retires the
    question — a cell is exactly as big as it is.

    Note it is NOT smaller on disk at slide scale, which a quick test on a small canvas
    suggests it should be: at this figure size and dpi the label panels land within a few
    percent of the scatter they replaced (~3.3 MB each). The saving only appears on a
    small, low-dpi canvas where contiguous regions compress well; blown up to a full
    slide there is enough boundary detail to erase it.

    render_labels, not render_shapes, though both can draw real cell outlines. The table
    annotates `cell_labels`, so labels work with no schema change, while colouring
    `cell_boundaries` by a QC column needs a second table keyed on cell_id. At this
    magnification a cell is about two points across, so the polygons' extra fidelity is
    not visible — it would only pay off zoomed in.

    One metric per slide, each with its own norm and colourbar. Sharing a scale across
    metrics is not an option even in principle here — genes top out near 2,400 on these
    ROIs against ~10,600 transcripts and 3% control — but the reason for a whole slide
    each is that these panels are read for spatial STRUCTURE, and a quarter-slide panel of
    a 21k-cell ROI is too small to see any. It makes for a long deck, which is the
    intended trade while the metrics are still being chosen.

    The norm follows the metric's scale, and getting it wrong is not cosmetic: a log norm
    over pct_control (0–3%) or nucleus_ratio (0–1) spends the whole ramp below 1 and
    masks the 87% of cells sitting at exactly 0, so the panel reads as empty tissue. A
    categorical metric takes no norm and no colormap at all — spatialdata_plot assigns a
    discrete palette and draws a legend instead of a colourbar.

    Zeros on a LOG panel are handled through the colormap rather than by clipping the
    data: a log norm masks non-positive values, and a masked pixel takes the colormap's
    "bad" colour, which defaults to transparent — those cells would silently vanish from
    the panel that exists to locate them. Painting `bad` with the bottom of the ramp keeps
    them visible without altering a value. Linear panels need none of this.

    The figure is sized here rather than by the library, because nothing in it can choose
    an orientation from the tissue's shape. A fixed size wastes the slide on anything that
    is not 2:1, since equal aspect is non-negotiable for tissue and a tall section renders
    as a sliver down the middle of a wide figure. These ROIs run both ways — one a 3:1
    strip, the other a 1:2.2 block — so the panel is fitted to each sample's own aspect,
    touching whichever edge of the slide's plot box binds first.

    Axis ticks are hidden rather than labelled. spatialdata's `global` frame for a Xenium
    read is in PIXELS — cell_labels maps to it with an identity transform while the
    boundary polygons carry a 4.7059 scale — so the numbers on these axes are not µm and
    would be actively misleading. The squidpy version carried a µm scale bar instead;
    restoring one here needs the pixel size, which nothing in the object records where
    this function can reach it.
    """
    display(Markdown(f"## In tissue — {label}"))
    display(Markdown(
        f"Each cell drawn at its segmented shape and position, coloured by {label.lower()}"
        + (" on a log colour scale. Cells at zero are painted the bottom of the ramp."
           if scale == "log" else
           " on a discrete palette, one colour per category." if scale == "categorical"
           else " on a linear colour scale.")
        + " The panel is at tissue proportions with an equal aspect."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0], FIGSIZE[1]))

    # Solid fill, no outline: at this magnification a cell is a couple of points across,
    # so an outline would be most of it and the default alpha only muddies the colour it
    # is there to show.
    render = dict(color=color, fill_alpha=1.0, outline_alpha=0.0)
    if scale == "log":
        values = table.obs[color].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        positive = values[np.isfinite(values) & (values > 0)]
        cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
        # See the docstring: masked (non-positive) pixels would otherwise be transparent.
        cmap.set_bad(cmap(0.0))
        render |= {"cmap": cmap,
                   "norm": SafeLogNorm(vmin=positive.min(), vmax=positive.max())}
    elif scale != "categorical":
        values = table.obs[color].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        render |= {"cmap": "viridis",
                   "norm": Normalize(vmin=np.nanmin(values), vmax=np.nanmax(values))}

    sdata.pl.render_labels("cell_labels", **render).pl.show(ax=ax, title="")

    # The aspect is read back from the drawn limits rather than computed from
    # obsm["spatial"]: the two agree here (2.8568 either way, since the label raster is
    # cropped to the cells), but the limits are what the axes will actually honour.
    fit_tissue_panel(fig, ax, abs(np.ptp(ax.get_xlim()) / np.ptp(ax.get_ylim())))

    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    # See the docstring: these axes are in pixels, not µm.
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

    # No tight_layout: see fit_tissue_panel.
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells", x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def transcript_map_slide(sdata, sample, element, label, vmax, size, n_molecules, share):
    """Slide: where a subset of the molecule table sits in tissue, by spatialdata_plot.

    The only spatial view in this deck drawn from transcripts rather than from cells, and
    that is the point of it: everything on the tissue slides is already conditioned on
    segmentation, so a molecule that was never assigned to a cell is invisible there. Here
    it is not.

    Every map is this one call over a different element — same colormap, same reduction,
    same clip semantics — so the four read against each other and only the molecules
    change. That is why the subsets are registered as separate points elements rather than
    passed as a colour column: it keeps the call identical instead of branching on mode.

    Drawn as a COUNT per canvas point, through the continuous colour path so it carries a
    colourbar (see MAP_COUNT_COLUMN), and clipped at `vmax` rather than scaled to the
    data. The clip is the encoding, not a cosmetic: at a low vmax every occupied canvas
    point saturates, which turns the map into presence-versus-absence — the right form for
    a slide read for LOCATION rather than magnitude. The whole-table map takes a higher
    vmax because its information is the density variation itself.

    `method` is named rather than left to the library's >10,000-point rule, since the
    reduction is meaningless under the matplotlib path. `size` is not a marker size here;
    see MAP_POINT_SIZE.

    n_molecules and share are passed in rather than counted here, so all four subsets come
    from one dask pass at assembly. They are stated because the map answers WHERE and not
    HOW MUCH — a clipped count map is deliberately close to presence/absence, so its
    magnitude cannot be read off the colour, and the share of transcripts assigned to no
    cell is the one segmentation figure nothing else in the pipeline reports.

    Two consequences of letting the library aggregate, both deliberate and neither hidden:

    The canvas resolution is the FIGURE's — figure inches x dpi — not a length in microns,
    so the effective bin changes with figure size and dpi, two samples of different extent
    are not strictly comparable, and `vmax` has to be re-tuned if either changes.

    These axes are spatialdata's `global` frame, which for a Xenium read is in pixels —
    the points element is stored in µm but carries a scale TO that frame — so the ticks
    are hidden here exactly as they are on the label slides, and there is no scale bar.
    """
    display(Markdown(f"## In tissue — {label}"))
    display(Markdown(
        f"Every transcript {'in this sample' if element == 'transcripts' else label.lower()}"
        ", counted over the plotting canvas, across the whole imaged area rather than only "
        f"within cells. The colour scale is clipped at {vmax}, so anything at or above that "
        "is drawn the same; white is where no transcript falls. "
        + (f"{n_molecules:,} transcripts in total."
           if element == "transcripts"
           else f"{n_molecules:,} transcripts, {share:.1%} of the sample.")
    ))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=FIGSIZE)
    sdata.pl.render_points(
        element, color=MAP_COUNT_COLUMN, method="datashader",
        datashader_reduction="count", size=size, cmap=MAP_CMAP,
        norm=Normalize(vmax=vmax),
        # Without this the colourbar is labelled with the raw column name.
        colorbar_params={"label": "Transcripts per canvas point"},
    ).pl.show(ax=ax, title="")

    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    # See the docstring: this frame is in pixels, not µm.
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

    fit_tissue_panel(fig, ax, abs(np.ptp(ax.get_xlim()) / np.ptp(ax.get_ylim())))

    # No tight_layout: see fit_tissue_panel.
    n = int(sdata.points[element].shape[0].compute())
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {n:,} transcripts", x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def gene_rank_slide(sdata, sample, gene_category=None):
    """Slide: the panel's genes ranked by total transcripts.

    The dynamic range of the panel in one line, and the only view that shows both ends of
    it at once. The histogram slide gives the same numbers as a distribution, but a rank
    curve is what makes the shape of the tail legible — where abundance falls off a cliff,
    and how much of the panel sits in the floor.

    Rank on a linear axis against abundance on a log one, because rank is a position in a
    list of 5,101 and abundance spans five decades. Genes no cell detected are at zero and
    cannot be drawn on that axis; they are the point of the slide rather than a footnote,
    so they are marked as a span at the foot of the curve and counted in the annotation.

    The curve itself stays one colour — it is a single ordering, and a line cannot carry a
    per-point category without becoming a scatter and losing the shape that is the reason
    to draw it. The minority categories are marked ON it instead, as points at their own
    rank, which answers where in the panel's dynamic range they fall. Predesigned genes
    are left unmarked because they are the curve: marking 4,995 of 5,101 points would
    redraw the line in a second colour and say nothing.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Gene abundance, ranked"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Every gene on the panel ranked by its total transcripts across all cells, on a "
        "log axis. Genes from a minority codeword category are marked at their rank. "
        "Genes detected in no cell have no abundance to draw and are marked as a band at "
        "the foot of the curve."
    ))

    var = sdata.tables["table"].var
    totals_raw = var["total_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    # One ordering used for both the curve and the marks, so a mark sits at the rank the
    # curve gives it. Sorting the values separately would put them at different positions.
    order = np.argsort(totals_raw)[::-1]
    totals = totals_raw[order]
    positive = totals[totals > 0]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.72, FIGSIZE[1]))
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, len(positive) + 1), positive, color=BAR_FILL, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    ax.set_yscale("log")

    if gene_category is not None:
        cats = gene_category.to_numpy(dtype=object)[order]
        drawable = totals > 0
        # Everything except the dominant category, which IS the curve — see the docstring.
        minority = [c for c in set(cats[drawable]) if c != "predesigned_gene"]
        for cat in sorted(minority, key=lambda c: -int((cats[drawable] == c).sum())):
            mask = drawable & (cats == cat)
            ax.scatter(np.flatnonzero(mask) + 1, totals[mask], s=7,
                       color=CATEGORY_INK.get(cat, UNMAPPED_INK), linewidths=0, zorder=3,
                       label=f"{str(cat).replace('_', ' ')} ({int(mask.sum()):,})")
        if minority:
            ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=7, markerscale=1.6)

    n_zero = len(totals) - len(positive)
    if n_zero:
        # Spanned rather than plotted: these genes have a rank but no drawable value, and
        # a band says "the list continues to here with nothing in it" where a dropped tail
        # would just end the curve early and look like the panel stopped at 5,071.
        ax.axvspan(len(positive), len(totals), color=ANNOTATION_INK, alpha=0.10)
        ax.annotate(f"{n_zero:,} genes in no cell",
                    xy=(len(totals), 0), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                    xytext=(-4, 12), textcoords="offset points",
                    ha="right", color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=7.5)

    ax.set_xlabel("Gene rank")
    ax.set_ylabel("Transcripts across all cells")
    ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(totals):,} genes", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def gene_detection_slide(sdata, sample, gene_category=None):
    """Slide: abundance against the number of cells detecting each gene.

    The gene-side counterpart of the transcripts-vs-genes scatter, and it separates the
    two ways a gene can be rare. A gene low on both axes is simply not expressed here. A
    gene with many transcripts in few cells is the shape that matters — either genuinely
    restricted to a small population, or a probe piling up on something that is not real.
    Neither margin alone tells them apart.

    Coloured by codeword category, which on the gene axis means predesigned against custom
    panel probes. That is the question this slide can answer and the histograms cannot:
    custom probes are designed separately from the catalogue ones, so whether they land in
    the same abundance-detection cloud or off to one side is a statement about the panel
    build rather than about the tissue. They are 100 of 5,101 here, so they are drawn LAST
    and larger — plotted in index order they would be buried under the predesigned cloud
    and the slide would show nothing.

    Drawn with matplotlib rather than sc.pl.scatter, which reads obs and var of an AnnData
    by name and is built for the cell axis; there is no var-side equivalent, and a plain
    scatter of two var columns needs nothing scanpy provides.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Gene abundance vs detection"))
    display(Markdown(
        "One point per gene: total transcripts across all cells against the number of "
        "cells detecting that gene, both on log axes, coloured by the category of codeword "
        "the gene is decoded from. Genes at zero on either axis cannot be drawn on a log "
        "axis and are counted in the title instead."
    ))

    var = sdata.tables["table"].var
    x = var["n_cells_by_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = var["total_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    drawable = (x > 0) & (y > 0)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.72, FIGSIZE[1]))
    if gene_category is None:
        # The molecule table is where the categories come from, so a sample whose points
        # failed to load still gets the geometry, just in one colour.
        groups = [(None, drawable, BAR_FILL, f"{int(drawable.sum()):,} genes")]
    else:
        cats = gene_category.to_numpy(dtype=object)
        # Rarest category last, so the small ones land on top of the big ones. This is the
        # whole reason the slide is legible with a 50:1 class imbalance.
        order = sorted(set(cats[drawable]),
                       key=lambda c: -int((cats[drawable] == c).sum()))
        groups = [(c, drawable & (cats == c), CATEGORY_INK.get(c, UNMAPPED_INK),
                   f"{str(c).replace('_', ' ')} ({int((drawable & (cats == c)).sum()):,})")
                  for c in order]

    for i, (_, mask, colour, label) in enumerate(groups):
        # Small and semi-transparent for the bulk: 5,101 genes on a log-log plane pile up
        # along one arm, and opaque markers there read as a solid bar rather than a
        # density. The minority classes are drawn larger and opaque so they can be seen at
        # all against it.
        bulk = i == 0 and len(groups) > 1
        ax.scatter(x[mask], y[mask], s=4 if bulk else 9, color=colour,
                   alpha=0.45 if bulk else 0.9, linewidths=0, label=label, zorder=2 + i)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    if len(groups) > 1:
        ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=7, markerscale=1.6)

    ax.set_xlabel("Cells detecting the gene")
    ax.set_ylabel("Transcripts across all cells")
    ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    title = f"{sample} · {len(x):,} genes"
    n_dropped = int((~drawable).sum())
    if n_dropped:
        title += f" · {n_dropped:,} at zero"
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def undetected_genes_slide(sdata, sample, gene_category=None):
    """Slide: the genes no cell detected, named.

    The one slide in this deck that is a list rather than a figure, because the useful
    output here is which probes to look at, and a name cannot be read off a distribution.
    Every other slide says how many; this one says which.

    A gene appearing here is not necessarily a failure — a panel carries markers for
    populations a given section may not contain. It is a starting point for asking which,
    which is why the slide names them and stops rather than calling them failed.

    Grouped by codeword category, which sorts the list into two different questions. A
    predesigned gene absent from an ovary section is almost certainly a tissue statement.
    A custom probe absent is a panel-build statement, since it was designed for this
    experiment and something was expected to bind. Mixed into one alphabetical list the
    two are indistinguishable, and the custom ones are the minority that would be lost.

    A gene with no transcript ANYWHERE in the sample has no row in the molecule table and
    so no category to look up. That is not a failure of the lookup — it is a stronger
    statement than the rest of the list, since these genes are absent even before cell
    assignment, so they are grouped under their own heading rather than dropped.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Genes detected in no cell"))

    var = sdata.tables["table"].var
    undetected = sorted(var.index[var["n_cells_by_transcripts"].to_numpy() == 0])

    if not undetected:
        display(Markdown(
            f"Every one of the {len(var):,} panel genes was detected in at least one cell "
            f"in {sample}."
        ))
        return

    display(Markdown(
        f"{len(undetected):,} of the {len(var):,} panel genes carry no transcript in any "
        f"cell in {sample}, grouped by the category of codeword they are decoded from. A "
        "gene may be absent because the section lacks the population it marks, so these "
        "are named rather than called failures."
    ))

    if gene_category is None:
        groups = [(None, undetected)]
    else:
        lookup = gene_category.reindex(undetected)
        found = lookup.to_numpy(dtype=object)
        groups = [(cat, sorted(lookup.index[found == cat]))
                  for cat in sorted({c for c in found if c is not None})]
        unmapped = sorted(lookup.index[found == None])  # noqa: E711 — elementwise, not `is`
        if unmapped:
            groups.append(("no transcript anywhere in the sample", unmapped))

    # A plain comma-joined paragraph per group, not a table: pandoc's pptx writer gives a
    # table its own layout and a fixed column count, which wastes most of a slide on 30
    # short names and overflows silently past whatever count fills the frame.
    for cat, genes in groups:
        if not genes:
            continue
        if cat is not None:
            display(Markdown(f"**{str(cat).replace('_', ' ')}** ({len(genes):,})"))
        display(Markdown(", ".join(f"`{g}`" for g in genes)))


def transcript_qv_slide(sdata, sample, tx):
    """Slide: the decoder's quality score over every transcript in the sample.

    The rawest QC number the run has. qv is the Xenium decoder's confidence that a
    molecule was called correctly, on a Phred-like scale; QV_THRESHOLD (20, a 1% error
    rate) is the value Xenium's own pipeline treats as the boundary.

    That boundary has ALREADY been applied by the time this deck sees a count. 10x builds
    the cell-feature matrix only from molecules at qv >= 20, so transcript_counts is
    exactly the count of transcripts that are is_gene, assigned to a cell, and above the
    cut — verified on an uncropped test bundle, where it matches for 100.000% of cells
    while counting every molecule regardless of qv matches 0.27%.

    So the fraction below threshold is NOT a marginal tail inside the counts; it is the
    data discarded before counting, and it is what makes the slide worth its place. A
    sample that lost 30% of its molecules here will look sparse on every per-cell
    distribution for a reason that is not biological, and no other slide reports it.

    The distribution is strongly bimodal and saturates — most molecules land at exactly 40,
    the ceiling — so this is deliberately a linear axis over the full 0-40 range rather
    than anything adaptive. A log count axis, though, because the trustworthy mode is
    orders of magnitude taller than the tail that matters.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Transcript quality"))
    display(Markdown(
        "The decoder's quality value for every transcript in this sample, on a linear "
        f"axis over the full range. The dashed line marks qv {QV_THRESHOLD}, the cut "
        "Xenium applies when building the cell-feature matrix: molecules below it are "
        "excluded from the per-cell counts on the earlier slides. Counts are on a log axis."
    ))

    qv = tx["qv"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    below = float((qv < QV_THRESHOLD).mean())

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.72, FIGSIZE[1]))
    ax.hist(qv, bins=80, color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.axvline(QV_THRESHOLD, color=ANNOTATION_INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.annotate(f"{below:.1%} below qv {QV_THRESHOLD}",
                xy=(QV_THRESHOLD, 1), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                xytext=(4, -11), textcoords="offset points",
                color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=7.5)

    ax.set_xlabel("Transcript quality value (qv)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Transcripts")
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(qv):,} transcripts", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def codeword_category_slide(sdata, sample, tx):
    """Slide: how the run's molecules divide across codeword categories.

    The negative-control picture at the molecule level, which the per-cell pct_control
    cannot give: that column is a per-cell ratio over the five control counters lumped
    together, while these are the categories themselves, separated and counted.

    A log count axis, because the categories span five decades — millions of gene calls
    against a few hundred of each control class — and on a linear axis every control bar
    is invisible, which is the opposite of what a control is for.

    Horizontal bars for the same reason the segmentation-method panel uses them: the
    category names are long, and they belong on the axis with room for them.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Transcripts by codeword category"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Every transcript in this sample counted by the category of codeword it was "
        "decoded to, on a log axis. Gene categories are the panel's real targets; the "
        "control and unassigned categories are the run's background."
    ))

    counts = tx["codeword_category"].value_counts().sort_values()
    total = int(counts.sum())

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.78, FIGSIZE[1]))
    ax.barh(range(len(counts)), counts.to_numpy(),
            color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(counts)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([str(c).replace("_", " ") for c in counts.index], fontsize=7)

    # The share is the number being read here, and it is unreadable off a log axis —
    # two bars a millimetre apart differ by a factor of three.
    for i, n in enumerate(counts.to_numpy()):
        ax.annotate(f"  {n:,} ({n / total:.3%})", xy=(n, i), va="center",
                    color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=6.5)

    ax.set_xlabel("Transcripts")
    ax.grid(axis="x", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
    # Room for the annotations, which extend past the longest bar.
    ax.set_xlim(right=counts.max() * 12)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {total:,} transcripts", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def qv_by_category_slide(sdata, sample, tx):
    """Slide: the quality distribution of each codeword category separately.

    The control check the deck exists to make, and the one slide that says whether the
    decoder is working rather than what the tissue contains. Negative controls are
    codewords with no target to bind: if the run is sound they should decode rarely AND
    badly, so they belong at the low end of this axis. A negative control sitting at the
    same quality as the real genes means the decoder cannot tell them apart, which no
    per-cell metric anywhere else in this deck would reveal — those molecules are simply
    counted as background at a plausible-looking rate.

    Each category is normalised to its OWN share rather than plotted as raw counts. That
    is the whole point: the categories span five decades of abundance (5.4M predesigned
    genes against 162 negative-control probes), and on shared counts every control curve
    is a flat line on the floor. Normalising asks the only question that compares across
    them — what does a molecule OF THIS CLASS typically score — and makes 162 molecules
    as readable as five million.

    Step outlines rather than filled bars, because seven overlapping filled histograms
    hide each other whatever the alpha, and the shape is what is being compared.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Transcript quality by codeword category"))
    display(Markdown(
        "The distribution of quality values within each codeword category, each "
        "normalised to its own share of transcripts so categories of very different size "
        f"can be compared. The dashed line marks qv {QV_THRESHOLD}. The table gives each "
        "category's median and the share of it falling below that threshold."
    ))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.74, FIGSIZE[1]))
    bins = np.linspace(0, 40, 60)
    rows = []
    # Largest first, so the legend order matches the category bar slide and the eye can
    # carry an ordering between the two.
    for cat, group in sorted(tx.groupby("codeword_category", observed=True),
                             key=lambda kv: -len(kv[1])):
        qv = group["qv"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        ax.hist(qv, bins=bins, histtype="step", linewidth=1.3,
                color=CATEGORY_INK.get(cat, UNMAPPED_INK),
                weights=np.full(len(qv), 1.0 / len(qv)),
                label=str(cat).replace("_", " "))
        rows.append((str(cat).replace("_", " "), len(qv), float(np.median(qv)),
                     float((qv < QV_THRESHOLD).mean())))

    ax.axvline(QV_THRESHOLD, color=ANNOTATION_INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("Transcript quality value (qv)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Share of the category's transcripts")
    ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=6.5)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(tx):,} transcripts", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)

    # The medians as a table, on their OWN slide with its own heading. Seven overlapping
    # step curves show the shapes but cannot be read to a number, and the median and the
    # sub-threshold share are the two numbers that get quoted off this slide.
    #
    # The heading is explicit because pandoc puts a table on a fresh slide regardless —
    # a figure and a table do not share one under this template — so without it the table
    # arrives untitled and detached from the figure it belongs to.
    display(Markdown("## Transcript quality by codeword category, in numbers"))
    display(Markdown(
        "| Category | Transcripts | Median qv | "
        f"Below qv {QV_THRESHOLD} |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n"
        + "\n".join(f"| {name} | {n:,} | {median:.1f} | {share:.1%} |"
                    for name, n, median, share in rows)
    ))


def transcript_fov_slide(sdata, sample, tx):
    """Slide: transcript yield and quality per field of view.

    The only slide in this deck that can see an INSTRUMENT problem rather than a biological
    or segmentation one. A field that lost focus, or that decoded badly on one cycle, shows
    up as a low bar here while being invisible in every per-cell distribution — its cells
    just look like poor cells, spread through the same histograms as everything else.

    Both panels share the same field order so a field can be read across them. Yield alone
    is ambiguous: a field covering the edge of the section legitimately holds fewer
    transcripts, and it is a normal yield with a depressed median qv, or the reverse, that
    points at the instrument rather than the tissue.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Transcripts by field of view"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Left, the number of transcripts decoded in each field of view. Right, the median "
        "quality value in the same field, with the dashed line at Xenium's default "
        f"threshold of qv {QV_THRESHOLD}. Fields are in the same order in both panels."
    ))

    by_fov = tx.groupby("fov_name", observed=True)
    counts = by_fov.size().sort_index()
    median_qv = by_fov["qv"].median().reindex(counts.index)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=FIGSIZE, squeeze=False)
    for ax, values, label in ((axes[0, 0], counts, "Transcripts"),
                              (axes[0, 1], median_qv, "Median qv")):
        ax.bar(range(len(values)), values.to_numpy(),
               color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(values)))
        ax.set_xticklabels([str(f) for f in values.index], fontsize=6.5, rotation=90)
        ax.set_xlabel("Field of view")
        ax.set_ylabel(label)
        ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        ax.tick_params(length=0)
        ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

    axes[0, 1].axhline(QV_THRESHOLD, color=ANNOTATION_INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(counts):,} fields · {len(tx):,} transcripts",
                 x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def transcript_geometry_slide(sdata, sample, tx):
    """Slide: where the molecules sit relative to the tissue and the nuclei.

    Three views of assignment rather than of expression, and they answer questions the
    cell-level slides cannot reach because a molecule assigned to the wrong cell still
    counts as a transcript in that cell.

    The z panel is a focus check: the section occupies a band of z-planes, and transcripts
    piling up at one end mean the imaged volume was not centred on the tissue.

    The nucleus-distance panel is a segmentation check at molecule resolution. Cells are
```
